name: Posterolateral approach to the talus
corridor: Incision just lateral to the Achilles, not over the tendon, through pre-Achilles fat with FHL protecting the posterior tibial bundle medially, then vertical ankle and subtalar capsulotomies

positioning.text: Position so the lateral Achilles border, calcaneal tuberosity, and posterior ankle can be seen and a tibia–calcaneus distractor can be applied.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the lateral aspect of the Achilles tendon and the calcaneal tuberosity. Keep the cut off the Achilles and posterior to the sural nerve.

incision.text: Incise just lateral to the Achilles, not over the tendon. This is the vertical limb of an extended lateral calcaneal cut and can be lengthened farther than a typical extended-lateral vertical limb.

superficial_interval.text: Stay posterior to the sural nerve, especially superiorly. Deepen lateral to Achilles paratenon through pre-Achilles fat. Respect the lateral calcaneal artery, which supplies most of this skin.

deep_interval.text: Medially the FHL belly protects the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle. Incise the ankle and subtalar capsules vertically to show distal tibia above, calcaneus below, and the talar body between them. A distractor or external fixator between tibia and calcaneus widens the window.

layers.text: Skin, sural-nerve and lateral-calcaneal-artery plane, Achilles paratenon and pre-Achilles fat, FHL, then posterior ankle and subtalar capsules and the posterior talar body.

structures_at_risk.text: The sural nerve, Achilles tendon, and lateral calcaneal artery are the local structures at risk. Compared with a posteromedial window this cut does not put the posterior tibial bundle in the field.

danger_zones.text: A cut over the Achilles or too far anterior toward the sural nerve, and injury to the lateral calcaneal artery, are the danger zones.

retraction_hazards.text: This is a deep window to the back of the talus. Do not retract through FHL into the posterior tibial bundle, and do not expect a proximal extensile interval because FHL blocks it.

exposure.text: Shows the posterior half of the talar body, the posterior distal tibia and fibula, and the posterior calcaneus.

limitations.text: Dissection to the back of the talus is deep, and the approach is not extensile proximally because of FHL. It does not show the anterior half of the body.

indications.text: Used for acute posterior talar fractures, nonunion surgery, and posterior stabilization of a reduced talar neck.

complications.text: Complications include sural neurapraxia, Achilles-tendon injury, and lateral-calcaneal-artery compromise of the posterior skin.

procedure_applications.condition: A posterior talar-body fracture or nonunion is fixed, or a reduced talar neck is stabilized from behind

questions.question: Where is the posterolateral talar incision placed relative to the Achilles?
questions.answer: Just lateral to the Achilles, not over the tendon, using the lateral Achilles border and calcaneal tuberosity as landmarks.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of this window over a posteromedial approach?
questions.answer: It does not put the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle in the field.

questions.question: Why is the approach not extensile proximally?
questions.answer: Flexor hallucis longus blocks proximal extension.
